A B S T R A C T
To address the frequent occurrence of safety accidents in process industries and the inadequacy of traditional
safety management approaches in coping with complex risk scenarios, this study proposed an intelligent question
answering system based on graph retrieval-augmented generation, named GRAG-ProSafe QAS. The system
adopted a four-stage framework to extract structured knowledge from accident reports using Large Language
Models and constructed a dynamic knowledge graph. This graph is utilized to support multi-hop retrieval and
chain-of-thought reasoning strategies, thereby enhancing the trustworthiness of the generated responses. Taking
198 accident reports from the iron and steel industry as the dataset, the experiments demonstrated that the
model achieved efficient structured knowledge extraction, and the constructed knowledge graph covers 1637
nodes with 2285 edges, which can provide semantic support for multi-hop causal reasoning. Ablation experi
ments validated the effectiveness of each core module in the system such as structured graph retrieval. In the
multi-turn question answering scenario focused on explosion accidents, the system achieved strong overall
performance, with a Faithfulness Score of 0.8684, Answer Relevancy of 0.8241, and Factual Correctness of
0.8050. The developed GRAG-ProSafe QAS realized the integration of knowledge extraction, graph construction
and intelligent QA, which provides a feasible path for the intelligent management and control of safety risks in
the process industry.

In this study, we proposed and developed a Graph Retrieval-
Augmented Generation system for Process Production Safety Intelli
gent Question Answering (GRAG-ProSafe QAS), as illustrated in Fig. 2.
The system integrated dynamic knowledge graph construction and
multi-hop causal reasoning to support interpretable risk discovery and
multi-scenario decision-making. It extends traditional QA by incorpo

efficient and adaptive knowledge extraction in dynamic safety

(2) We develop a multi-turn reasoning strategy that integrates multi

of single-pass retrieval in existing RAG + KG models and improves
factual accuracy and domain relevance in complex queries.
(3) We designed and implemented an intelligent QA system that
supports entity-relation extraction, accident cause analysis, hazard
identification and safety recommendations, thereby improving the in
telligence level of enterprise safety management.

2.1. Process production safety risk management
As a key national economic pillar, the process industry has long
relied on systematic engineering for safety risk management, with core
methods like HAZOP and FMEA, combined with industrial safety stan
dards, forming risk control systems widely used in steel and chemical
sectors to build a relatively comprehensive accident prevention archi

2.2. Knowledge extraction based on large language model
Knowledge extraction is a key subfield of Natural Language Pro
cessing (NLP) that aims to derive structured information from unstruc
tured text. It typically involves Named Entity Recognition (NER),
Relation Extraction (RE), and Event Extraction (EE). Recent advances in
large language models, with their large parameter scales and powerful
architectures, have greatly enhanced the accuracy and generalization of
knowledge extraction tasks(Xia et al., 2025). Current mainstream
extraction techniques include prompt design(K. Zhang et al., 2023), few
shot learning(Y. Liu et al., 2024), supervised fine-tuning (Zhou et al.,
2022) and data augmentation(Q. Wang et al., 2023). As shown in
Table 1. However, knowledge extraction often encounters challenges
such as long-text processing and cross-sentence reasoning in real-world
industrial scenarios. To address these limitations, researchers have
explored hybrid strategies. For instance, Yang et al. (2024) proposed a
knowledge extraction method for the water conservancy domain (DTKE-
LLM), which integrates prompt learning with fine-tuning of LLMs. Wan
et al. (2023) designed task-specific prompt templates with predefined
entity types and reasoning demonstrations, achieving state-of-the-art
results on SciERC. Dong et al. (2025) extended extraction beyond text,
proposing a multimodal method that integrates textual and visual in
formation from incident reports. These studies highlight the advantages
of LLM-based extraction in improving precision and generalization. The
resulting structured knowledge plays a crucial role in downstream tasks
such as knowledge graph construction(L. Zhong et al., 2023), machine
translation(Zhu et al., 2023), knowledge reasoning(S. Zhang et al.,
2025) and intelligent question answering(Luo et al., 2018).
2.3. Retrieval-augmented generation method
Despite their strong natural language generation capabilities, LLMs
may produce incorrect responses when addressing queries beyond their
training data, a phenomenon known as hallucination(Bang et al., 2023).
Retrieval-Augmented Generation mitigates this by retrieving relevant
external knowledge to address domain-specific limitations, using it as
contextual input for generation, thereby enhancing factual consistency

RAG improved knowledge reliability and reduced hallucinations by

and trustworthy responses. Bahr et al. (2025) converted FMEA records

3.1.2. Entity recognition
Entity recognition serves as the foundation for constructing knowl
edge graphs. Given that accident reports often follow a standardized
narrative structure, the fine-grained extraction of key elements using
predefined entity types can substantially enhance the accuracy of sub
sequent relation inference. Based on accident causation theory, this
study defined six major entity types. Each major type is further refined
into specific subtypes. For example, unsafe human behaviors are divided
into four subcategories: safety awareness, material control, equipment
operation and protective measures. These categories are tailored to
reflect the characteristics of process industries while reducing semantic
ambiguity. In total, 32 subcategories are defined, as summarized in
Table 2.
Prompt engineering for large language models involves guiding the
model’s attention and generation behavior by designing specific
prompts, with the aim of eliciting desired outputs for downstream tasks.
The process begins with role assignment, where the model is instructed
to act as an accident analysis expert, enabling it to identify key infor
mation from a domain-specific perspective. Next, a task description
explicitly defines the recognition objectives and procedural steps to
ensure the output remains concise. Finally, the use of few-shot learning
with illustrative examples is essential. By providing concrete examples
of entity extraction from accident reports, the model can better under
stand the task expectations, thereby enhancing the accuracy and con
sistency of its outputs. This process is illustrated in Fig. 4.

4.2. Performance evaluation of the RAG
4.2.1. Verification of the developed models
In this section, multiple-round QA tasks are designed, where the
system extracts the keywords of the user’s question in each round, and
supplements the relevant real triples missing after the last round of
retrieval of the graph through graph retrieval, in order to strengthen the
coherence of the reasoning chain and the comprehensiveness of the
answers. Using an explosion accident as a case study, the model’s ability
to identify systematic failure chains, refine causal relationships and
generate in-depth explanations is assessed through step-by-step ques
tioning and reasoning analyses, as illustrated in Fig. 10. In the first
round, the system adopted the Human-Equipment-Environment-
Management framework to summarize the systemic accumulation
characteristics of accident-inducing factors, and pointed out that ex
plosion accidents were often triggered by a combination of multiple
factors, including operator misconduct, equipment defects, high-
temperature confined environments and managerial lapses. This
response demonstrated the system’s ability to generalize multifactorial
causes and their interaction mechanisms, thereby laying a causal foun
dation for subsequent deep reasoning. In the second round, the system
analyzed the evolution mechanism of the accident and abstracted a
three-tier failure path comprising instantaneous causes, institutional
deficiencies and root causes. It revealed a nonlinear evolution pattern

4.2.2. Cross-Model Evaluation: Automated and expert Assessments
To ensure the robustness, generality, and practical utility of the
proposed multi-turn QA system, this section conducted a cross-model
evaluation that integrates automated metrics and expert reviews. In
addition to DeepSeek-V3, we incorporated two other high-performance
LLMs: Qwen-plus (Apr 2025 release) and Doubao-1.5-pro-32 k (Jan
2025 release) for entity and relation extraction, knowledge retrieval,
and final answer generation. To mitigate potential evaluation bias
caused by model homogeneity, we selected GPT-3.5-turbo, a model
known for its consistency and robustness in general-purpose evaluation
tasks, to assess the quality of response content across models. A dual
evaluation strategy was adopted. We constructed a set of ten represen
tative QA cases, each focusing on common causation scenarios in the
process industry. All generated responses were independently evaluated
by five domain experts specializing in process safety and accident
analysis. These experts hold either PhDs or senior engineering titles in
relevant fields and have an average of 12.4 years of practical experience.
The expert evaluation followed the same three dimensions as the auto
mated metrics: Faithfulness, Factual Correctness, and Answer Rele
vancy. The scores were normalized to the [0,1] range for comparison
with automated results and the Likert-scale evaluation framework is
summarized in Table 6.
As illustrated in Fig. 11, the automated scores across all three LLM
remained consistently stable across the three metrics, validating the
system’s transferability and reproducibility. Taking DeepSeek-V3 as an
example, its Faithfulness score of 0.8468 indicates that the majority of
responses were well-grounded in retrieved knowledge. A Factual Cor
rectness score of 0.7968 reflects strong logical and technical accuracy,
while an Answer Relevancy score of 0.8356 suggests a high degree of
contextual alignment with user intent. The largest gap appeared in
Faithfulness, suggesting automated metrics may overestimate
grounding quality. Factual Correctness and Answer Relevancy showed
closer agreement, indicating that the system’s reasoning and contextual
alignment were largely consistent across evaluation methods. In sum
mary, while automated metrics are generally reliable, expert judgment
remains crucial in safety–critical domains. The integration of multiple
LLMs and cross-model evaluation significantly enhances the reliability
and applicability of the findings.

4.2.4. Design and application of GRAG-ProSafe QAS
In this study, we designed and developed a graph retrieval and
enhancement generation system named GRAG-ProSafe QAS, which
adopts a front-end and back-end separation architecture, the front-end
was built using the Vue3 framework, featuring a clean and efficient
user interface, while the back-end employed FastAPI to handle task
scheduling and integrated a Neo4j graph database for knowledge graph
storage and retrieval. The system interface was structured into two core
modules: the Entity-Relationship Extraction Module (EREM) and the
Graph-based Retrieval Augmented Generation Module (RAGM), which
respectively supported knowledge graph construction and multi-turn
question answering tasks. As illustrated in Fig. 12, the system work
flow proceeded as follows:
In EREM, users could import accident report texts via direct input or
file upload. The system then invoked DeepSeek-V3 to perform entity
recognition and relation extraction, presenting the results as structured
triples, which could be seamlessly imported into the knowledge graph
with a single click. Taking the February 23, 2024 poisoning and
asphyxiation accident in Lvliang City as a case, the system successfully
identified 13 entities and 14 triples, covering accident attributes and
unsafe human behaviors. Upon successful graph import, a correspond
ing notification would be generated on the front end. In RAGM, the
system allowed users to initiate multi-turn question answering tasks
based on specific objectives. It generated more accurate and structured
responses by leveraging contextual information from the knowledge
graph. After each round, the system automatically evaluated the quality
of the generated answers using metrics such as Faithfulness and Answer
Relevancy, assisting users in intuitively understanding the QA
performance.
Overall, the GRAG-ProSafe QAS achieved the integration of accident
knowledge extraction, graph construction and question answering
evaluation. With its high interactivity and structured knowledge support
capabilities, the system provides a practical and scalable technical so
lution for advancing intelligent safety control and management in the
process industry.
5. Conclusion and future work
This study proposes a knowledge graph–augmented question
answering system for process safety scenarios. By integrating automatic
knowledge extraction with retrieval-augmented generation techniques,
the system enables structured representation and interpretable
reasoning over process safety knowledge. The main conclusions are as
follows:(1) A four-stage knowledge extraction framework was devel
oped to efficiently construct structured knowledge graphs from accident
reports in the steel industry; (2) In multi-turn question answering tasks
related to explosion accidents, the system demonstrated strong perfor
mance in terms of faithfulness, accuracy, and relevance, confirming the
effectiveness of the graph-enhanced reasoning approach;(3) Case studies
showed that the system supports multi-turn causal chain analysis,
structured knowledge output, and automated evaluation, indicating its
practical value and scalability for supporting safety-related decision-
making.
Despite the above achievements, this study has several limitations.
Firstly, system evaluation was conducted on static historical accident
reports, without experimental validation of its performance in real-time
or streaming scenarios, limiting the verification of its dynamic update
capability. Secondly, the system lacks qualitative error analysis, and
specific failure cases in entity recognition and reasoning processes were
not systematically identified, hindering targeted optimization. Thirdly,
the model’s cross-domain generalization ability remains untested, and
the domain-specific nature of accident reports may affect the robustness
of knowledge extraction and reasoning.
To address these limitations, future research will focus on three
directions:
(1) Evaluating system performance in real-time or streaming envi
ronments by simulating incremental data flows or integrating time-
series sensor data. This will help verify system responsiveness in sce
narios such as continuous data ingestion, incremental entity recognition,
and rapid relation fusion, with key metrics including graph update la
tency and system response time.
(2) Conducting systematic error analysis of critical modules such as
entity recognition and multi-hop reasoning. Expert annotation or clus
tering methods will be used to categorize typical failures such as relation
hallucination and broken reasoning chains. These insights will inform
iterative refinement of relation confidence calibration strategies and
prompt template designs to enhance robustness and reasoning quality.
(3) Intend to collect accident reports and regulatory data from
petrochemical and related industries, and, with expert annotations,
construct industry-specific subgraphs for supervised fine-tuning of the
pre-trained model. In parallel, apply embedding alignment and relation
mapping to build a cross-domain semantic mapping mechanism,
improving entity and relation adaptation in heterogeneous domains.

In EREM, users could import accident report texts via direct input or
file upload. The system then invoked DeepSeek-V3 to perform entity
recognition and relation extraction, presenting the results as structured
triples, which could be seamlessly imported into the knowledge graph
with a single click. Taking the February 23, 2024 poisoning and
asphyxiation accident in Lvliang City as a case, the system successfully
identified 13 entities and 14 triples, covering accident attributes and
unsafe human behaviors. Upon successful graph import, a correspond
ing notification would be generated on the front end. In RAGM, the
system allowed users to initiate multi-turn question answering tasks
based on specific objectives. It generated more accurate and structured
responses by leveraging contextual information from the knowledge
graph. After each round, the system automatically evaluated the quality
of the generated answers using metrics such as Faithfulness and Answer
Relevancy, assisting users in intuitively understanding the QA
performance.
Overall, the GRAG-ProSafe QAS achieved the integration of accident
knowledge extraction, graph construction and question answering
evaluation. With its high interactivity and structured knowledge support
capabilities, the system provides a practical and scalable technical so
lution for advancing intelligent safety control and management in the
process industry.
5. Conclusion and future work
This study proposes a knowledge graph–augmented question
answering system for process safety scenarios. By integrating automatic
knowledge extraction with retrieval-augmented generation techniques,
the system enables structured representation and interpretable
reasoning over process safety knowledge. The main conclusions are as
follows:(1) A four-stage knowledge extraction framework was devel
oped to efficiently construct structured knowledge graphs from accident
reports in the steel industry; (2) In multi-turn question answering tasks
related to explosion accidents, the system demonstrated strong perfor
mance in terms of faithfulness, accuracy, and relevance, confirming the
effectiveness of the graph-enhanced reasoning approach;(3) Case studies
showed that the system supports multi-turn causal chain analysis,
structured knowledge output, and automated evaluation, indicating its
practical value and scalability for supporting safety-related decision-
making.
Despite the above achievements, this study has several limitations.
Firstly, system evaluation was conducted on static historical accident
reports, without experimental validation of its performance in real-time
or streaming scenarios, limiting the verification of its dynamic update
capability. Secondly, the system lacks qualitative error analysis, and
specific failure cases in entity recognition and reasoning processes were
not systematically identified, hindering targeted optimization. Thirdly,
the model’s cross-domain generalization ability remains untested, and
the domain-specific nature of accident reports may affect the robustness
of knowledge extraction and reasoning.
To address these limitations, future research will focus on three
directions:
(1) Evaluating system performance in real-time or streaming envi
ronments by simulating incremental data flows or integrating time-
series sensor data. This will help verify system responsiveness in sce
narios such as continuous data ingestion, incremental entity recognition,
and rapid relation fusion, with key metrics including graph update la
tency and system response time.
(2) Conducting systematic error analysis of critical modules such as
entity recognition and multi-hop reasoning. Expert annotation or clus
tering methods will be used to categorize typical failures such as relation
hallucination and broken reasoning chains. These insights will inform
iterative refinement of relation confidence calibration strategies and
prompt template designs to enhance robustness and reasoning quality.
(3) Intend to collect accident reports and regulatory data from
petrochemical and related industries, and, with expert annotations,
construct industry-specific subgraphs for supervised fine-tuning of the
pre-trained model. In parallel, apply embedding alignment and relation
mapping to build a cross-domain semantic mapping mechanism,
improving entity and relation adaptation in heterogeneous domains.
